nameStory: This plant earned its "purplestem" name from the reddish-purple coloring that often develops on its stems, especially as the season progresses. The "beggarticks" part comes from its clingy seeds that grab onto clothing and animal fur with tiny hooks, like a persistent beggar that won't let go!
description: Purplestem Beggarticks is a tall annual wildflower that can tower up to 6-7 feet high in favorable conditions. It produces small, bright yellow daisy-like flowers with both a central disc and short petals (ray flowers). This wetland plant has a sturdy, upright growth habit and opposite leaves that clasp the stem, making it a common sight in marshes and wet meadows throughout New England.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems are smooth and often develop a distinctive reddish-purple tint, especially on the upper portions and as the plant matures - run your finger along the stem to feel its smooth texture

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flower heads about 1/2 inch across with short, inconspicuous yellow petals surrounding a yellow center disc - often only 1-3 flower heads per plant

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are lance-shaped with toothed edges and connect directly to the stem without leaf stalks - they feel slightly rough and papery when rubbed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, wedge-shaped seeds topped with 2-4 barbed bristles that grab onto clothing with a scratchy grip - shake a mature flower head and listen for the rattling seeds

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright annual that can reach 3-6 feet high with a sturdy main stem and few branches, often growing in dense patches

habitat: Look for Purplestem Beggarticks in marshes, wet meadows, pond edges, and ditches throughout New England's lowlands. It thrives in areas that stay consistently moist or occasionally flood, often growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll rarely find it far from water sources or in well-drained upland areas.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their first opposite leaves appearing smooth and green.
seasonality.summer: Rapid upward growth occurs with stems elongating and developing their characteristic purple tinting by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Yellow flowers bloom from August through October, followed quickly by the clingy seeds that disperse on clothing and animal fur.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist as brown stalks, but the annual plant has completed its life cycle and died back completely.

funFact: Despite being called "beggarticks," this plant is actually more generous than greedy - its flowers provide late-season nectar for migrating monarch butterflies when few other blooms remain, making it a crucial pit stop on their journey south!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other beggarticks species, but Purplestem is the only one that consistently develops that telltale purple stem coloring. Memory trick: "Purple stem, purple name" - if you see purple on the stem, you've found the right beggarticks!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - while these seeds are clingy hitchhikers, the plant itself is a valuable native species that supports pollinators and wildlife. The "ticks" in the name refers to the seeds' resemblance to actual ticks when they're stuck to your socks!
compareHints: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant. Devil's Beggarticks has hairy stems and more divided leaves, while Nodding Beggarticks has flower heads that droop downward rather than standing upright.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
